title: Workshop overview
content:
Introduction CloudDocs is an enterprise document management system that has been developed and integrated with AWS services. The project uses Amazon EC2 for the application environment, Amazon RDS MySQL for business data, Amazon S3 for private document storage and Amazon Cognito for user authentication.
This workshop presents the architecture, configuration steps and practical results of the system. Screenshots in the following sections illustrate AWS settings and functions exercised in CloudDocs.
Workshop objectives Understand the roles and relationships of EC2, RDS MySQL, S3, Cognito and IAM in the system. Understand environment configuration, service connections and application deployment. Explain sign-in, upload, preview, download and document authorization flows. Compare practical results using AWS configuration, application screens and activity logs. Architecture overview The HTML, CSS and JavaScript frontend communicates with the Spring Boot backend through REST APIs. The backend connects to RDS MySQL for metadata and business data, verifies identities issued by Cognito and creates presigned URLs for direct browser-to-S3 file transfers. An IAM role and bucket policy authorize cross-account S3 access as shown in the diagram.
Main processing flows The user signs in through Cognito using Authorization Code + PKCE; the frontend receives an access token. The frontend sends REST API requests with a Bearer token; the backend validates the JWT and checks the account and role in MySQL. For upload, the backend creates metadata, checks the quota and issues a presigned PUT URL; the browser sends the file directly to S3. The frontend confirms completion; the backend checks the object with HeadObject and updates the document size. For preview or download, the backend checks current permissions and issues a time-limited presigned GET URL. Sharing, trash, restore, task assignment and report review are handled by the backend; business records and activity logs are stored in MySQL. Completed functionality The system includes sign-in and sign-out, document management, upload, preview, download, search, permission-based sharing, favorites, trash and restore. User management, storage statistics, activity logs, notifications and the task assignment – report submission – approval workflow have also been added to the application.
Practical illustrations of these functions appear in 4.8. Business and integration testing. The configuration sections below combine procedural guidance with screenshots from the practice environment so that readers can compare each architecture component.

title: Proposal
content:
This section presents CloudDocs — Enterprise document management on the AWS cloud.
CloudDocs — Enterprise document management on AWS A solution combining Spring Boot, MySQL, S3 and Cognito 1. Executive summary CloudDocs centralizes documents and work-processing workflows in a web application. ADMIN manages accounts, documents and announcements; USER manages owned or shared documents. Java 21/Spring Boot 3.5.6 provides REST APIs and authorization; HTML/CSS/JavaScript provides the frontend; MySQL stores metadata, sharing relationships, quotas and business audit records. Files are stored in private S3, with authentication through a Cognito User Pool.
The target architecture uses EC2 for the application and Nginx, RDS MySQL for the database and an IAM role for S3 access. The application uses S3 for documents, Cognito for authentication and MySQL for business data.
2. Problem statement Current problems
Documents scattered across personal devices or chat channels are difficult to find, authorize and trace to the person who changed them. Accidental deletion, excessive sharing, missing capacity controls and disconnected assignments and reports reduce traceability.
Solution
CloudDocs organizes documents by metadata and department and supports search/filtering, preview, download, permission-based sharing, favorites and trash. The backend checks permissions before issuing time-limited URLs; files move directly between the browser and S3. MySQL stores business data and audit records. Assignment creation, report submission, approval and change requests are extensions available in the early-November release.
Benefits and return on investment (ROI)
Reduce manual searching and sharing; measure the time required for the same scenario before and after adoption. Separate file contents from metadata for clearer data management and fewer file transfers through the backend. Use trash and audit records to handle mistakes; apply account quotas to control allocations. Financial ROI and savings rates have not been measured. Costs are modeled from assumptions and compared with Billing during deployment. 3. Solution architecture AWS services used or planned for operation
Category Component Role and status Compute Amazon EC2, Nginx Application server environment; EC2 connectivity has been established Database Amazon RDS for MySQL Metadata, users, permissions and audit; RDS MySQL connectivity has been established Storage Amazon S3 Private bucket, signed PUT/GET and object confirmation; integrated in the code Identity Amazon Cognito User Pool PKCE sign-in and access token issuance; integrated in the code Security/network IAM Role, VPC, Security Group Resource permissions and network restrictions configured per environment Operations CloudWatch, Budgets Resource monitoring, log collection and budget tracking Component design
Frontend: static web interface; the Cognito public client has no client secret. Configure callback, logout and API_BASE for each environment. Backend: validate JWTs, read current roles/status from MySQL, check owner_id and document permissions, and manage upload state and quotas. RDS/MySQL: store users, documents, permissions, favorites, notifications, audit and work_tasks according to the current schema. S3: UUID object keys; original names remain in metadata. Workflow: metadata → signed PUT → S3 PUT → upload-complete/HEAD; signed GET is issued after authorization. Cognito: link identities by issuer/sub rather than email; distinguish ADMIN/USER system roles from OWNER/VIEW/DOWNLOAD/EDIT document permissions. Legacy local workflow: local file endpoints remain for compatibility. The current frontend uses S3; this does not imply that every historical file has been migrated. 4. Technical implementation Implementation stages
Analyze business needs, study AWS and design the permission matrix. Develop the ERD, backend/frontend and metadata APIs; manage source code with Git. Integrate private S3, CORS, presigned URLs, sharing and audit; prepare test cases. Prepare EC2/RDS, the IAM role, Nginx configuration and environment variables. Integrate Cognito and run integration tests according to actual progress; extend quotas, trash and work-task workflows in the following stage. Technical requirements
Java 21, Maven, MySQL 8 and Node.js for serving the frontend/testing; the frontend is not React and has no npm build step. A valid base schema and any missing incremental migrations. The application uses ddl-auto=validate and does not create an empty database automatically. AWS account, S3 bucket, Cognito pool/client/domain and RDS endpoint; EC2 and an IAM role when deploying to AWS. Keep passwords, access keys, tokens and client secrets out of the repository. Deployment database connections require TLS; local settings must not be copied unchanged to AWS. 5. Roadmap and milestones Week Period Topic Learning outcome 1 10/08/2026–14/08/2026 AWS accounts, Budgets and Support Understood initial AWS account setup and protection. 2 17/08/2026–21/08/2026 AWS IAM and access management Distinguished users, groups, policies and roles. 3 24/08/2026–28/08/2026 Amazon VPC and network components Understood basic VPC components. 4 31/08/2026–04/09/2026 Amazon EC2 and virtual servers Understood launching and connecting to EC2. 5 07/09/2026–11/09/2026 Managing EC2, EBS and snapshots Distinguished instance lifecycles, EBS volumes, snapshots and AMIs. 6 14/09/2026–18/09/2026 Amazon S3 and AWS CLI Understood the bucket/object model and the AWS CLI’s role. 7 21/09/2026–25/09/2026 S3 security, CORS and presigned URLs Explained private bucket protection and presigned URLs. 8 28/09/2026–02/10/2026 Amazon RDS and MySQL databases Understood RDS MySQL components and connection parameters. 9 05/10/2026–09/10/2026 Amazon RDS backups and security Explained backups, snapshots, restoration and the purpose of Multi-AZ. 10 12/10/2026–16/10/2026 Amazon Cognito and user management Understood User Pools, app clients and sign-in configuration. 11 19/10/2026–23/10/2026 Cognito authentication flows and JWTs Explained Cognito authentication flows and token roles. 12 26/10/2026–30/10/2026 Relationships between AWS services Described an application architecture using the AWS services studied. 6. Budget estimate Demo assumptions: one EC2 instance, one Single-AZ RDS MySQL instance, 5 GB of S3 files, 20 GB of EBS, approximately ten users and 160 infrastructure operating hours per month for learning. These are modeling assumptions, not measured usage or an AWS quotation.
Item Calculation for AWS Pricing Calculator EC2 compute Hourly instance price × 160 hours; compare with 730 hours for continuous operation EBS 20 GB × price per GB-month, including periods when EC2 is stopped RDS compute Hourly DB instance price × actual operating hours RDS storage/backup Allocated capacity × price per GB-month, plus billable backups/snapshots S3 5 GB-month + PUT/GET/HEAD requests + actual data transfer Public IPv4 and networking Number of IPs × billable hours; add NAT Gateway or endpoints if used Cognito Monthly active users and the account’s selected features/tier CloudWatch/Budgets Log volume, retention, metrics/alarms and selected budget features Domain/HTTPS Include only selected services; do not assume Route 53/ALB is used Total Sum all items using the Region, configuration and prices at the estimation date The budget depends on Region, resource configuration, operating time and prices at deployment. Estimates are prepared with AWS Pricing Calculator, while actual usage is tracked through AWS Billing. Storage, snapshots and IP addresses are accounted for separately according to the configuration.
7. Risk assessment Risk matrix
Risk Impact Qualitative likelihood S3 failures caused by incorrect IAM, CORS or Region High Medium RDS connection failure or incorrect schema High Medium Incorrect callback, issuer or app client High Medium Metadata/object inconsistency after failed uploads High Medium Previously issued URLs remain valid after permission revocation Medium A property of the current design Repeated migrations or execution against the wrong database High Medium Charges from retained resources Medium Medium Mitigation strategy
Keep the bucket private, scope the IAM role to the required prefix, authorize requests in the backend and use short-lived URLs. Back up the database, preflight migrations, verify objects with HEAD and test with different accounts. Restrict security groups to permitted sources, use TLS for RDS and keep secrets outside source code. Track costs and clean up demo resources after use.
Contingency plan
Retain the previous build, database backup and controlled environment configuration. If EC2 is unavailable, demonstrate the local application connected to authorized services and identify the demonstration environment accurately. Do not restore a database over active data without a controlled procedure; test restoration on a separate copy first.
8. Expected outcomes Technical improvements
Demonstrate sign-in, upload, preview/download, sharing/revocation and audit using both system roles. Verify quotas, trash, restoration and permanent deletion against metadata/S3. Demonstrate assignments, report submission, pending approval, change requests and late submission in the extended release. Provide deployment instructions, environment configuration and test scenarios matching the actual source code. Long-term value
Develop skills in backend engineering, authentication, authorization, relational data, object storage and independent architecture research. Possible extensions include automated deployment, improved resilience, file scanning, report versioning and monitoring; count them as completed outcomes only after implementation.
References First Cloud AI Journey AWS Documentation The internship outline and CloudDocs technical documentation.

title: IAM, VPC and secure connectivity
content:
1. Select the account and network Identify the account/Region and add Project=CloudDocs and Environment=demo tags to supported resources. Use an appropriate existing VPC or create a lab VPC: EC2 needs a subnet with suitable outbound connectivity; RDS needs a DB subnet group covering subnets in at least two Availability Zones. A Single-AZ RDS instance still requires a valid subnet group.
2. Security groups Group Intended inbound access Notes clouddocs-web-sg Port 443 from users; port 80 for redirects/certificate issuance if needed Nginx terminates TLS; do not expose port 8080 clouddocs-db-sg Port 3306 from clouddocs-web-sg Do not expose MySQL to the entire Internet Administration Session Manager with the required permissions/connectivity; IP-restricted SSH if needed Session Manager does not work without its prerequisites A private RDS instance cannot be reached directly from a laptop over the Internet. Use an authorized administrative path such as a tunnel, SSM, VPN or operations from EC2; do not make it public simply to bypass a network error.
3. EC2 IAM role Create a role trusted by EC2 and attach a policy scoped to the project’s bucket/prefix. Replace ACCOUNT/BUCKET for the deployment environment before applying the example:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:ListBucket","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::YOUR_BUCKET","Condition":{"StringLike":{"s3:prefix":["documents","documents/*"]}}}, {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject","s3:DeleteObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::YOUR_BUCKET/documents/*"} ] } Attach the role using an instance profile; the backend uses the default credential provider chain. HeadObject requires GetObject permission. SSE-KMS requires appropriate KMS permissions and key policy. Do not send AWS access keys to the frontend.
4. Cross-account access, if applicable Configure this only for the actual deployment accounts. AssumeRole requires the trust policy, sts:AssumeRole permission and matching credential flow; a policy on only one side is insufficient. Direct resource-policy access requires checking both the role and bucket policies. This is an environment-dependent deployment option, not an assumed existing configuration.
Verification: EC2 reaches RDS through the correct security groups; the backend has Get/Put/Delete access to the project prefix; public origins cannot access database/backend ports.
Practice and illustrated results T02. EC2 IAM role Open EC2 → Instances → select the instance → Security to inspect the IAM role and security groups. The screenshot records CloudDocsEc2Role attached to the administration bridge instance.
T03. EC2 security group inbound rules Open the security group → Inbound rules. The pictured clouddocs-ssm-ec2-sg allows HTTP on port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. This records a demo configuration; it does not demonstrate HTTPS or a review of every group attached to the instance.
T04. S3 access policy contents In IAM, inspect the policy allowing GetObject, PutObject and DeleteObject on clouddocs-dev-private/documents/*. The screenshot shows the policy editor and documents the intended permissions; verify that the saved policy is attached to the role when validating access.
T05. Role trust relationship Open IAM → Roles → CloudDocsEc2Role → Trust relationships. The ec2.amazonaws.com principal and sts:AssumeRole allow EC2 to assume the role; S3 operations are separately governed by permission and bucket policies.

title: Private S3 and CORS configuration
content:
1. Create or verify the bucket In the S3 Console, select the project bucket in the agreed Region. Keep Block Public Access, Bucket owner enforced Object Ownership and default encryption enabled. Review existing data before changing an active bucket. Do not enable public website hosting for the document bucket.
The backend uses the documents/ prefix and UUID keys. Policy, CORS and script examples are in Back_end/aws/s3. Running these tools changes infrastructure; they are not mandatory application startup steps.
2. Configure CORS for the actual origin Example for S3 Console → Permissions → CORS; replace the origin:
[ { "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD", "PUT"], "AllowedOrigins": ["https://YOUR_FRONTEND_HOST"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 3600 } ] The Console expects the array of rules shown above. AWS CLI JSON wraps rules in a CORSRules object, as in the repository example. For local development, add the exact active origin, such as http://localhost:5500 or http://127.0.0.1:5500. CORS does not replace IAM or make a bucket public.
3. Backend configuration Variable Required value AWS_REGION Actual bucket Region S3_BUCKET The project’s bucket name S3_PRESIGN_EXPIRY Lifetime in seconds; current default is 900 and may be reduced as required 4. Test the normal workflow Sign in and create metadata with POST /api/documents. Call POST /api/documents/{id}/upload-url; use the current UI/DTO rather than guessing JSON fields. The frontend sends the File with PUT to the S3 URL, preserving signed headers. Call POST /api/documents/{id}/upload-complete; the backend verifies the object with HEAD and confirms its size. Request GET preview-url/download-url using an authorized account and open the newly issued URL. Expected result: the private object exists, metadata confirms the upload and unshared accounts are denied access. Previously signed URLs may remain usable until expiration; temporary credential expiration can invalidate them earlier.
Common errors For HTTP 403, check the signing principal, policy, prefix, Region, headers and expiration. For CORS, compare the complete scheme/host/port origin and test in a browser. When metadata exists but the file is missing, do not treat the upload as complete; handle the pending allocation through the application workflow.
See CORS and presigned URLs.
Practice and illustrated results H01. Bucket and Region Open S3 → Buckets. The clouddocs-dev-private bucket is in Asia Pacific (Singapore), ap-southeast-1; configure the backend S3 client for this Region.
H02. Block public access Under Permissions, Block all public access is On and Object Ownership is Bucket owner enforced. Documents use authorized access rather than a public bucket website.
H03. Cross-account bucket policy The bucket policy allows CloudDocsEc2Role in account 861358180788 to read, write and delete objects under documents/*. Compare the role ARN with T02/T05 and its permission policy. This is resource-policy access, not evidence that the application assumes a separate S3 role.
H04. Saved CORS configuration Under Permissions → CORS, the saved configuration allows GET, PUT and HEAD from http://54.255.190.1; ExposeHeaders contains ETag and Content-Disposition, and MaxAgeSeconds is 300. This is the origin recorded at capture time; synchronize it when the frontend host or port changes.
H05. Default SSE-S3 encryption Open Properties → Default encryption. The encryption type is SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys; this is not an SSE-KMS configuration.
H06. Stored objects under documents/ Open Objects → documents/ to compare keys, file types, sizes and modification times. The list contains both older and newer test keys; it does not imply that every object was created by the same application version.
H07. Individual object properties Select DeCuongThucTapChuyenNganh.docx → Properties. The screenshot records a documents/ key, a 36.9 KB size, Standard storage and SSE-S3; Bucket Versioning is Disabled. These properties complement the H06 object list.

title: RDS MySQL, schema and migrations
content:
1. Prepare RDS Create or verify a MySQL instance compatible with the application in the RDS Console. Select the prepared VPC/subnet group and database security group; configure storage, backup retention and password management for the environment. Describe a Single-AZ lab accurately rather than calling it Multi-AZ. Record the endpoint, port and schema name in configuration management.
2. Import the base schema The repository does not include a complete empty-database installer. Use a verified schema export, check for sensitive data and import into a test database first. Base business tables such as users/documents/audit_logs must exist. Do not apply incremental migrations to an empty database or enable ddl-auto=update merely to bypass validation failures.
3. Review migrations Order File in Back_end/db/migration Purpose 0 00_PRECHECK.sql Check legacy owner references 1 01_APPLY_document_permissions.sql owner_id and sharing permissions 2 02_APPLY_document_favorites.sql Favorites 3 03_APPLY_notifications.sql Global announcements 4 04_APPLY_cognito_identities.sql issuer/sub identity mapping 5 05_APPLY_optional_contact_email.sql Optional contact email 6 06_APPLY_work_tasks.sql Work tasks and recipient notifications; part of the November update Apply only missing steps after backing up and preflighting the correct database. Migration 04 and share-cognito-identities.sql are alternative ways to create the same table; do not run them consecutively. MySQL DDL may commit automatically, so ROLLBACK does not undo every ALTER/CREATE.
4. Connect the application Set DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD outside source code. Give the application user only required privileges and keep it separate from the migration administrator.
TLS: the current application.yml contains a local JDBC URL with useSSL=false. For AWS, override SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL with an RDS JDBC URL using sslMode=VERIFY_IDENTITY and configure the correct RDS CA bundle/JVM truststore. Verify the SSL session; changing DB_HOST alone does not establish encryption.
5. Verification Start the backend with the verified schema and confirm that ddl-auto=validate reports no missing tables/columns. Perform authorized test reads/writes, check metadata/audit and capture results with sensitive information hidden. Test backup restoration on a separate database before claiming recovery has been verified.

T08. RDS endpoint and networking In Connectivity & security, record the endpoint, port 3306, VPC, subnets and security groups. Publicly accessible is Yes in the screenshot, so this does not demonstrate the recommended private RDS setup described above. Actual reachability also depends on networking rules and routes.
T09. Database security group MySQL rule Open rds-ec2-1 → Inbound rules. The pictured rule accepts MySQL/Aurora TCP 3306 from an EC2 security group. Review the other groups attached to the database as well; one group screenshot does not describe all effective network permissions.
T10. RDS connection and data query In the MySQL client, inspect the connection to the RDS endpoint and the company_documents database. SHOW TABLES lists business tables including users, documents, document_permissions, audit_logs and work_tasks. SELECT id, title, file_type, file_size, created_at FROM documents WHERE id IN (35, 36, 37) ORDER BY id returns three document records, illustrating metadata reads from the database. These are the pictured test records and are not assumed to be the same file as H07. title: Feedback and Suggestions
content:
Reflections on the learning process Studying First Cloud AI Journey materials helped me approach AWS topics in sequence, from account and cost management to permissions, networking, compute, storage and databases.
Maintaining a weekly worklog helped me divide the material into manageable topics, track my progress and identify concepts requiring further review. This showed me the value of clear objectives and regular note-taking.
Helpful aspects of the materials The topics introduce several groups of AWS services. Diagrams help beginners understand relationships between components. Sample configurations support technical explanations. Security and cost management topics encourage responsible resource use. Learning difficulties Networking, IAM policies and container configuration required repeated reading. With limited practical experience, I sometimes found it difficult to visualize how all the components work together.
English documentation required additional vocabulary research. Since service information can change, learners need to check official documentation before applying instructions.
Suggestions for the materials Include a Vietnamese–English glossary for each topic. State prerequisite knowledge at the beginning of each lesson. Add review questions and explanations of commonly confused concepts. Indicate update dates and changes affecting instructions. For practical exercises, identify resources, permissions, potential costs and cleanup steps. Include common error scenarios and guidance on researching their causes. Suggestions for learning support I would welcome more beginner-focused discussions explaining diagrams, terminology and documentation reading strategies. Topic-based question-and-answer sessions could help learners consolidate their knowledge.
For practical sessions, I suggest small exercises with clear objectives and cost controls. Learners could then summarize their results and discuss remaining questions.
Acknowledgements I would like to thank the internship organization, mentors and the First Cloud AI Journey community for the opportunity to study AWS.
The knowledge and study methods gained provide a foundation for continued learning, practical experience and professional development.

title: Cognito and user authentication
content:
1. User Pool and public app client Create or verify the User Pool, domain and web app client. Use a public client without a client secret, Authorization Code grant and PKCE. Callback/logout settings must exactly match actual URLs; use HTTPS for deployment. Select scopes appropriate to UserInfo, usually openid, profile and email according to the application. Do not enable unnecessary grants.
2. Consistent configuration Location Configuration FrontEnd/js/cognito-config.js Domain, client ID, redirectUri/logoutUri and scopes using the actual file structure Backend COGNITO_ISSUER_URI Issuer https://cognito-idp.REGION.amazonaws.com/POOL_ID Backend COGNITO_CLIENT_ID Corresponding public app client ID Backend COGNITO_USER_INFO_URI UserInfo domain for the actual pool Backend CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS Actual frontend origin Do not copy the development issuer/client into another pool’s configuration. Read the values assigned by local scripts rather than assuming externally supplied environment variables remain unchanged.
3. Backend validation and internal identities The backend validates the JWT signature, issuer, validity period, token_use=access, client_id and sub. The system maps issuer/sub to a MySQL account and reads its current role/status. Email and full name are profile data, not substitutes for the identity key.
New accounts receive USER. Review Back_end/db/bootstrap-cognito-admin.sql to bootstrap the first ADMIN; do not arbitrarily edit shared database data. The template defaults to NULL targets/ROLLBACK so the operator can inspect it first.
4. Testing Test sign-in, callback, GET /api/auth/me and logout. Missing, invalid or expired tokens must be rejected; USER must not call administrative APIs; locked/DELETED accounts must be denied business access. Logout does not instantly invalidate every access-token copy; document the actual behavior accurately.
See Cognito PKCE.
Practice and illustrated results S01. User Pool overview Open Cognito → User pools → the application pool. Compare the Pool ID and us-east-1 Region when configuring the issuer; this Region differs from S3/RDS.
S02. Frontend app client Choose App clients → clouddocs-web. Client secret is shown as a dash, consistent with a client without a secret. The React selection in the Console quick-start guide does not establish the actual frontend technology used by the project.
S03–S04. Callback, logout, grant and scopes In Login pages, inspect callback/logout URLs, the Authorization code grant and email, openid and profile scopes. The screenshot records localhost/127.0.0.1 URLs for local use; deployment requires registering the actual frontend URLs. A grant configuration screenshot alone does not prove that the browser performed PKCE.
S05. Sign-in domain Open Branding → Domain and use the pool domain to synchronize the application authorize, token, UserInfo and logout configuration.
S06. Cognito test users Open Users to inspect accounts, Email verified, Confirmation status and Enabled status. CloudDocs ADMIN/USER roles are managed in application data and cannot be inferred from Cognito Confirmed status.

title: EC2, Nginx and operations
content:
1. Prepare the server Create or verify an appropriate Linux EC2 instance, S3 instance profile and network security group. Install Java 21 and Nginx using packages appropriate to the OS. Build the JAR in a verified environment and transfer it and FrontEnd to the server. The current frontend needs neither npm install nor npm build. Do not serve the entire repository through the web server.
2. Backend environment configuration Keep configuration in an environment file readable only by the operator, outside the web root and repository. Minimum variables:
Variable Purpose SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=aws Deployment profile DB_HOST / DB_PORT / DB_NAME / DB_USERNAME / DB_PASSWORD Database connection SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL TLS JDBC override described in the RDS section AWS_REGION / S3_BUCKET / S3_PRESIGN_EXPIRY Environment-specific S3 settings COGNITO_ISSUER_URI / COGNITO_CLIENT_ID / COGNITO_USER_INFO_URI Authentication against the correct pool CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS Frontend origin PORT=8080 Backend accessed only through the reverse proxy Replace paths and the actual JAR in this systemd example. Create the clouddocs system user first and grant it access to configuration and application files. An example JAR name is not a command that can be used unchanged in every environment.
[Unit] Description=CloudDocs backend After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] User=clouddocs WorkingDirectory=/opt/clouddocs EnvironmentFile=/etc/clouddocs/backend.env ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/clouddocs/backend.jar Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 SuccessExitStatus=143 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Rename the tested deployment build to backend.jar and verify that /usr/bin/java is Java 21. Run systemctl daemon-reload and enable/start according to the administration procedure, then inspect journalctl -u clouddocs for errors. Keep passwords/tokens out of logs.
3. Serve the frontend and proxy with Nginx Example inside an HTTPS server with a valid certificate; replace the domain, certificate and directories for the actual server:
root /var/www/clouddocs; index index.html; location / { try_files $uri $uri/ =404; } location /api/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; } Copy the contents of FrontEnd into the web root in this example. If the callback uses /FrontEnd/, preserve that prefix in directory/Nginx configuration; changing Cognito alone is insufficient. Set API_BASE for the actual hostname/backend. Run nginx -t before reloading. Redirect port 80 to HTTPS according to environment policy; a domain/certificate is a prerequisite rather than an assumed existing resource.
4. Monitoring, backups and costs Basic EC2 CloudWatch monitoring includes CPU, network and status checks. RAM, filesystem and application logs require the agent, permissions and suitable networking. Set retention, generate a controlled error and verify that its log arrives. Configure RDS backup/snapshot retention and test restoration on a copy. Set a budget with the appropriate account, recipient and threshold; Budgets is not a switch that automatically stops every resource.
Secrets Manager may be added later, but the application currently reads environment variables. Creating a secret does not automatically make Spring Boot retrieve it.
5. Deployment evidence Record the EC2 instance, commit/JAR, deployment time, HTTPS URL, /api/health, RDS connection, S3 upload and Cognito sign-in. Use endpoints, hostnames and screenshots from the actual CloudDocs environment under test.
Practice and illustrated results T01. EC2 in the practice environment EC2 → Instances records clouddocs-ssm-bridge-1b as Running, with a t3.micro type and passed status checks. Its private DNS ip-172-31-16-134 matches the hostname in T06; the terminal check below adds evidence of the backend service running on this instance at capture time.
T06. Running backend and health check In the EC2 terminal session, run hostname and date -Is to record the host and verification time. systemctl is-active clouddocs returns active; curl to http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator/health returns {“status”:“UP”} and HTTP 200. Hostname ip-172-31-16-134 matches the private DNS in T01, providing evidence that the backend was running on this instance at capture time. The pictured endpoint is /actuator/health; this result does not replace sign-in, file transfer or external access tests.

title: Business and integration testing
content:
Test prerequisites Prepare at least one ADMIN and two active USER accounts linked to Cognito, an authorized small file, an empty file and an oversized file for rejection tests. Use test data and record the commit, environment, tester and time. The following table lists scenarios and expected results, not preassigned passing outcomes.
ID Scenario Expected result AUTH-01 Missing, invalid or expired access token Business API rejects the request without exposing content AUTH-02 USER calls an administrative API Access denied DOC-01 Create metadata, PUT to S3 and confirm upload Object exists; metadata is correct and readable DOC-02 Concurrent uploads with identical filenames Distinct object keys; no unintended overwrite DOC-03 Failed/missing PUT followed by confirmation Missing object is not confirmed; allocation remains tracked DOC-04 Zero-byte file Preview/download handles the file appropriately for its format DOC-05 File exceeds 100 MiB or the account quota Rejected; allocations remain within the quota ACL-01 Grant VIEW to USER B B can preview but cannot obtain download/edit access ACL-02 Grant DOWNLOAD/EDIT Only the corresponding actions are allowed; sharing administration is not implied ACL-03 USER C has no share API denies preview/download/edit ACL-04 Revoke B’s permission New URL requests are blocked; previously issued URLs may remain valid until expiration TRASH-01 Owner moves a file to trash Preview/download/edit/share are blocked; quota still includes the file TRASH-02 Restore a file Returns to ACTIVE and preserves earlier shares as designed TRASH-03 Permanently delete a test file Object/permissions removed; metadata becomes PURGED with size 0; audit retained BULK-01 Select multiple files including one permission failure Show individual success/failure and allow retrying failed items QUOTA-01 Pending uploads, trash and shared documents Pending/trash count against the owner; sharing does not multiply allocation AUDIT-01 USER/ADMIN reads audit records USER sees their own actor events; ADMIN sees system-wide events TASK-01 ADMIN assigns work; USER submits a valid document Private notification and SUBMITTED/pending approval status TASK-02 Creator requests changes, then approves Only authorized actor proceeds; feedback, audit and notifications recorded TASK-03 Submit after the deadline Submission accepted and labeled late; reviewer delay does not make a pending approval overdue TASK-04 Two tabs use an outdated version HTTP 409; user must reload current data TASK-05 Delete/overwrite a SUBMITTED/COMPLETED report file API blocks the operation using the current release’s guard TASK-06 Delete one or multiple tasks Only the assigning ADMIN; retain documents/permissions/audit and handle related notifications USER-01 Delete an account with files or unfinished tasks Blocked according to current conditions Automated tests and limitations In the CloudDocs repository, run mvn -f Back_end/pom.xml test and node –test FrontEnd/tests/*.test.cjs. Tests using mock repositories/AWS clients do not verify live RDS migrations, row locking, Cognito redirects, S3 CORS or browser PDF rendering. Record results for each test execution.
Practice and illustrated results K01. Application after sign-in After sign-in, the Overview page displays the admin account and application navigation. This illustrates access to CloudDocs; authentication configuration is documented in the Cognito section.
K02a. Document upload Choose Upload document, submit a test file and inspect the resulting list. The screenshot shows a notification that one document was saved successfully.
K02b. File preview Select Preview for the TXT test file. Its contents appear in the application preview dialog.
K02c. File download Select Download and inspect the browser downloads list. The downloaded TXT file appears alongside the CloudDocs download notification.
K03. Shared documents Sign in as an employee and open Shared with me. Rows expose different controls: Preview only or additional Download/Edit actions. This illustrates UI permissions; API denial checks follow the scenarios above.
K04. Document in the trash Move the PDF to the trash and open Trash. The screenshot shows the document, deletion time, Restore and Permanently delete controls.
K05. Document restored Restore the file from K04 and return to Documents. The same PDF appears as Active with a successful 1/1 restore notification.
K06. Assigned task details Open task details to inspect the assignee, assigner, deadline and requirements. K06 shows VCB 111 with test data; it is a separate creation example, not the VCB 4123 task in K07–K08.
K07. Report awaiting review After an employee submits the test attachment for VCB 4123, the administrator opens its details to see Awaiting review status, the attachment, submission time and review controls.
K08. Report review result Approve the same task shown in K07. Its status changes to Completed and a confirmation appears; the pair illustrates the submission-to-approval transition.
K09. User management Sign in as admin and open Users to inspect accounts, departments, roles and status. Role/status controls are displayed for each row.
K10a. Storage management overview Sign in as admin and open Storage management. The screenshot records 12.27 MB used against the displayed 1 TB quota, 1.65 KB in the trash, a file-type breakdown and documents sorted by size. These are application statistics at capture time, not an Amazon S3 service limit.
K10b. Storage usage by account Scroll to Storage usage by account to compare names, roles, usage, quotas and utilization. The screenshot shows 100 GB quotas for users and 1 TB for admin accounts; trashed documents remain in the allocation list above.
K11. Activity log Open Activity log. The screenshot records actors and timestamps for upload, deletion, restore, report submission and approval, which can be compared with K04–K08.
K12. Document search Enter DeCuong in document search. Two matching filenames appear. The screenshot illustrates filename search, not filtering by file type or department.

title: Cleanup and handover
content:
Before cleanup Clean up only authorized demo resources. Check whether resources are still needed for the project through 28 November; do not remove shared infrastructure at the end of an individual workshop session. Inventory resource IDs, Regions/accounts, ownership and data to retain. This guide does not execute AWS resource deletions.
Handover Keep the commit/JAR and startup instructions, a secret-free configuration inventory, applied schema/migrations, test results and evidence. Store backups only in approved locations and test restoration on a copy. Signed URLs and access tokens are not handover materials.
Demo cleanup sequence after confirmation Stop application access/processes and record configuration that must be retained. Back up the database if needed, then remove the designated demo RDS instance; check final snapshots and retained backups for continuing charges. Handle identified S3 test files. If Versioning is enabled, review versions and delete markers separately; deleting the current object does not delete every version. Terminate demo EC2 instances when no longer needed; check retained EBS, snapshots and public IPv4/Elastic IPs. Delete demo Cognito pools/clients only when no longer used; retain any pool still used by the project. Review CloudWatch log groups/alarms, networking such as NAT/endpoints, IAM roles/policies and other resources actually created. Check Billing across Regions after updates propagate. Stopping EC2 does not eliminate charges for retained EBS, snapshots or allocated IPs. Expected result: a handover record and retained/deleted resource inventory. Do not claim zero costs before reconciling the bill.
